https://www.azernews.az/culture/262858.h.text: International guests explore National Art Museum [PHOTOS] 25 August 2026 14:16 (UTC+04:00) Laman Ismayilova Read more Ren Quanxiu, head of the Lu Xun Academy of Fine Arts, one of China’s leading art academies, and Yuri Stanbek Shygaev, a People's Artist of the Kyrgyz Republic, visited the Azerbaijan National Art Museum. During their visit, they explored the museum's permanent collections and temporary exhibitions. The guests toured the museum's main collections and exhibition projects, including "Treasury of Azerbaijani Art," "Azerbaijani Painting and Graphics of the 1920s–1980s," and "The Sixtiers: Azerbaijani Art Free from Conformism." They also viewed the international exhibition "Dialogue of Cultures: Kazakhstan – Azerbaijan," which highlights the artistic ties between the two countries, as well as "Chronicle of the City of Winds: Baku in the Works of Artists of the 19th–21st Centuries," an exhibition dedicated to the history and distinctive character of the Azerbaijani capital. During the tour, particular attention was given to the stories behind the creation of the works on display. The guests explored how Baku's architecture, everyday life and atmosphere have been reflected in the works of artists from different generations. The museum's extensive collection and diverse range of artistic styles attracted considerable professional interest from the visitors. The Azerbaijan National Art Museum regularly hosts a wide range of cultural and scholarly events. These events often bring together art historians, researchers, and curators to explore various aspects of national and international art history. They also provide a platform for presenting newly acquired artworks, discussing attribution studies, and highlighting the results of academic research. Founded in 1937, the museum also offers art connoisseurs some of the finest examples of Western European decorative and applied arts. Its permanent exhibition features over 3,000 items displayed across 60 rooms, while approximately 12,000 additional works are preserved in its storage collections. Visitors can explore masterpieces by Italian, French, German, and Polish artists, among others. Over the years, the museum has also successfully organized and hosted numerous high-level international exhibitions, presenting works by world-renowned artists. These initiatives have not only attracted art enthusiasts but have also played an important role in fostering cultural exchange between Azerbaijan and other countries. https://www.timesandstar.co.uk/news/2659.text: Charity 13-year-old climbs Scafell Pike three times in 15 hours Charity By Charlie Yates Reporter Share 0 Comments 4 Skip to next photo 1 / 1 Show caption 1 / 1 Share 0 Comments This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. A 13-year-old scout has climbed Scafell Pike three times in under 24 hours. Rafferty Phillips, from the 3rd Wigton Sea Scouts in west Cumbria, took on the challenge to raise funds for the 2027 World Scout Jamboree in Poland. Hoping to become the first young person to complete the feat, Rafferty aimed to raise part of the £3,500 needed to attend the global scouting event. He completed the climbs in around 15 hours, beginning at 9.25am on September 16. From left: May, Eben, and Rafferty. (Image: Kirsty Phillips) Rafferty said: "It was pretty easy for the first two ascents. "And then on the last one, the weather started going downhill." The challenge covered more than 2,700 metres of ascent—roughly equivalent to climbing Mount Olympus. Rafferty was joined by his friends Eben and May, and the challenge was supervised by qualified mountain leaders, including his father, Dave Phillips. He said the most difficult part was near the top of the mountain. He said: "Probably the top quarter [was the hardest], because it feels like it just goes on." The final climb was completed in darkness, with rain, hail, strong winds and low cloud reducing visibility. When asked about the conditions on the descent, Rafferty said: "Basically, pitch black." Rafferty during the ascent in the dark. (Image: Kirsty Phillips) The fundraiser has so far raised more than £500. Mr Phillips said: "We found a number of adults that have recorded completing this challenge, but we couldn't find any children, non-adults under the age of 18, that had completed that." Rafferty described the challenge ahead of time as "the biggest physical test of my life" and "a potential world-first effort." Safety was a top priority throughout the challenge. Mr Phillips said: "The encouragement was that we should have been over the last summit by midnight. That's when the weather was breaking." Despite the difficult conditions, Rafferty kept his sense of humour. His mother, Kirsty Phillips, said: "Oh, he did. He had a moment on the last one when he realised he forgot his Chocomel." The fundraising challenge will help Rafferty attend the World Scout Jamboree in Poland, a worldwide gathering of scouts held every four years and often described as the "Olympics of scouting." Around 50,000 young people are expected to attend, including 18 from Cumbria. The party makes its way to the summit through the mist. (Image: Kirsty Phillips) Rafferty secured his place after a selection process focused on teamwork and problem-solving skills. His father said the experience had already made a difference in his son’s confidence and outlook. Mr Phillips said: "The journey's been quite impressive from a year ago when he got selected to now to see the growth in confidence." He described Rafferty as a young person who enjoys the outdoors more than screens. Mr Phillips said: "I would say he's a general teenager, but he's almost a general teenager from the 1980s. "He's out and busy." With the Scafell Pike challenge behind him, Rafferty is already considering future adventures. He and his friends are looking into a rapid attempt on the Cumbria Way as their next test. Photograph: Parliament TV Cyberwar Ministers must be honest about Russian threat to UK, says former Foreign Office head Peter Ricketts calls for more resilience in protecting banking, energy and water systems from cyber-assaults Harry Taylor Sat 17 Oct 2026 06.19 EDT Last modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 06.52 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Ministers need to be honest with the British public about the immediate threat posed by Russia , which could soon lead to lives being lost, a former national security adviser has said. Peter Ricketts, who advised David Cameron when he was prime minister, became the latest figure to warn about the scale of the threat posed by “hybrid attacks” from Vladimir Putin’s forces. The peer, who is the former top civil servant in the Foreign Office, said banking systems, energy or water supplies could be targeted by Kremlin cyber-assaults. He called for further investment in resilience for key sectors. It comes in a week where the heads of MI5 and the British army have warned about the danger posed by Moscow. Lord Ricketts also dismissed Andy Burnham’s claim he wanted to be a “bridge” between the US and Ukraine. Relations between Washington and Kyiv deteriorated sharply this week after Donald Trump waived a number of economic sanctions on Russia and suggested Ukraine needed a new leader. Speaking to BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, Ricketts said: “I think they’ve really got to start a conversation with the British people about what may be coming, because not only is Putin trying to break morale in Ukraine, he’s also trying to undermine morale in European countries.” In response to a question over the impact of disruption by Russia, he added: “I’m not saying there’s going to be industrial war with tanks rolling across the north German plain. “But these hybrid attacks are getting more reckless, more dangerous. One day, people are going to land up being killed somewhere, and so we are going to have to look at responding in that sense and finding the money to do it.” Speaking about Burnham’s comments at prime minister’s questions this week saying he wanted to be a bridge between Washington and Kyiv, Ricketts said: “I don’t really go on this bridge business. I mean, I don’t think in Trump’s current mood there’s any influence that Britain can have in the short term.” Ricketts’s comments join those by the director general of MI5, Sir Ken McCallum, and the chief of the general staff, Gen Sir Roly Walker, in the last few days about Russia. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion Starlink access still not fully restored for Ukraine’s military, says Zelenskyy Read more On Tuesday, McCallum said MI5 was devoting more resources to combating threats from hostile states than it did during the cold war and described Russia as the “number one aggressor”. And on Friday, Walker told 700 troops at Catterick garrison in North Yorkshire that politicians would soon need to have a “frank conversation” about the “sacrifices” that would be needed to prioritise defence and security. Walker, a former special forces commander, said soldiers would probably need to fight in a war , given the “extreme jeopardy in the world at the moment”. The warnings come after a difficult week for Kyiv, with the US appearing to withdraw support. Trump said the decision to pause sanctions was in the US “national interest”, despite previously signing them into law in September. Last week, he lifted restrictions on Russian diesel amid spiralling fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections. He also suggested Ukraine needed a new president. Volodymyr Zelenskyy hit back this week during an EU summit, saying it was nice to be among “real leaders”. There are also concerns that the US has withdrawn intelligence sharing with Ukraine, leaving towns and cities across the country vulnerable to attack. Ricketts said the government should spend more money on protections for key infrastructure in Britain, including energy, transport, air traffic control and defence.
